scope: Choose the right diode model for a given circuit, solve series-diode loops, and locate the quiescent point where the diode curve meets the dc load line.
intuition: A diode model is a promise about how much accuracy you need: the ideal switch is fine for a 10 V loop, the 0.7 V battery is fine for a 10 mA bias point, and only the piecewise-linear or exponential model survives high current or small signals. The load line is the circuit talking back — it says which (V,I) pairs the resistor permits, and the Q point is where the device finally agrees.
concept: **Four models, four jobs.** (1) The **ideal diode** is a one-way switch: zero drop forward, open reverse. It answers 'is the diode on?' and is acceptable when the source is many volts so the drop is a small fraction — 10 V across 1 kohm gives 10 mA ideal against 9.3 mA practical, a 7% error. (2) The **practical (constant-drop) model** adds a 0.7 V battery for silicon (0.3 V Ge/Schottky, 2 V for a red LED, 3.4 V for a white one). It is the workhorse for bias and rectifier work. (3) The **piecewise-linear model** adds a bulk resistance $r_B$ in series with that battery, $V_D = V_{knee} + I_Dr_B$, which is essential once the current is large enough for the ohmic regions to matter. (4) The **small-signal (dynamic) model** replaces the diode by $r_d = nV_T/I_{DQ}$ about the operating point and is valid only for swings of a few millivolts.

**The load line is just KVL drawn on the diode's axes.** For a source $V_{DD}$, a series resistor $R_L$ and a diode, KVL gives $V_{DD} = I_DR_L + V_D$, so $I_D = (V_{DD} - V_D)/R_L$ — a straight line with intercepts $(V_D = V_{DD}, I_D = 0)$ and $(V_D = 0, I_D = V_{DD}/R_L)$ and slope $-1/R_L$. Those two numbers are free and worth writing down first: the open-circuit end and the short-circuit end bracket every possible answer, so any computed current above $V_{DD}/R_L$ is instantly recognisable as wrong. The **Q point** is the intersection of that line with the device curve — nonlinear, so it is found graphically, by iteration, or by the constant-drop approximation.

**Why the approximation is usually good enough — and when it is not.** Because the diode curve is nearly vertical once it turns on, the intersection is insensitive to small errors in the assumed drop: using 0.7 V where the true drop is 0.597 V understates the current by only about 1% when $R_L = 1\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$. Narrow the resistor and the load line steepens: at $R_L = 100\ \Omega$ the same 0.1 V error in the diode drop is a 1 mA error out of ~94 mA, and the $r_B$ term (0.2 V at 20 mA for a 10 ohm diode) becomes comparable to the knee itself. Conversely, when the signal is *smaller* than the knee voltage — a 50 mV sensor output driving a diode — the constant-drop model is useless because the diode never 'turns on' in that picture, while the real device is a perfectly linear 26 ohm resistor at 1 mA. Choosing the model is really the question 'is my signal big compared with 0.7 V, or small compared with 26 mV?'

**Circuits with several diodes and LEDs.** Series diodes add their drops: two silicon junctions in a 12 V loop drop 1.4 V, and mixing materials means adding the right knees (0.7 + 0.3 for Si + Ge). Parallel diodes do *not* share current equally — the one with the lower drop (or the hotter one, because the forward voltage has a $-2\ \mathrm{mV/^\circ C}$ coefficient) takes almost everything, which is why current sharing needs series ballast resistors. For light-emitting diodes the design equation is the same KVL, $R = (V_S - V_F)/I_F$, but the answer must also be checked for resistor power, $P_R = I_F^{2}R$, and for the fact that $V_F$ is a nominal value that varies with current, colour and temperature — designing at exactly the rated 20 mA with a 5% resistor tolerance can push the LED over its limit. Back in the diode-only case, the operating point also *slides along the load line* as the device heats, because the whole curve shifts left by about 2 mV per degree.

formulas.n: Diode treated as a closed switch. Acceptable only when the real drop is a small fraction of V_DD, say under 5%.
V_knee = 0.7 V for Si, 0.3 V for Ge/Schottky, 2 V for a red LED. The standard bias/rectifier model.
Bulk resistance belongs in the denominator. Necessary above about 10 mA or when r_B is given.
Just KVL rearranged. Slope is -1/R_L, so a small R_L means a steep line and a Q point that is very sensitive to the knee.
Compute these first. Any answer outside this box is arithmetically impossible, which makes them a free error check.
The circuit constraint, true regardless of which device model you use. The device curve supplies the second equation.
Valid for signal swings of a few mV only, and it depends on the dc bias current, not on the signal.
Drops add in series; the current is common. Mixed materials need their own knee voltages, not one blanket 0.7 V.
Check P_R = I_F^2 R and pick the next standard value upward for safety. V_F is nominal.
Size to at least twice the calculated dissipation for a comfortable margin.

problems.prompt: A silicon diode is in series with a $1\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$ resistor across a $10\ \mathrm{V}$ dc source. Find the loop current with (i) the ideal-diode model and (ii) the practical constant-drop model.
steps: KVL check: $9.3 + 0.7 = 10\ \mathrm{V}$. The ideal model overstates the current by 7.5%.
problems.ans: Ideal: 10.0 mA. Practical: 9.3 mA with 9.3 V across the resistor.
problems.trap: Using the ideal model when the drop is a large fraction of the source. Here 0.7 V out of 10 V is 7%, tolerable; the same model on a 1.5 V source would claim 1.5 mA instead of 0.8 mA — an 88% error — because the diode drop is now half the supply.

steps: One line with `ALPHA` `:` — `10÷1000 : (10−0.7)÷1000` → **10.0** mA ideal → **9.3** mA practical.
calc.note: The same ideal model on a 1.5 V source is 88 % high; judge by the ratio $V_{knee}/V_{DD}$.

problems.prompt: The same $10\ \mathrm{V}$, $1\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$, silicon-diode loop now uses a diode with a bulk resistance $r_B = 10\ \Omega$. Find the current and the total diode voltage.
steps: $I_D = 9.208\ \mathrm{mA}$ (against 9.3 mA for the constant-drop model, only 1% less).
problems.ans: I_D = 9.21 mA; V_D = 0.792 V (0.700 V knee plus 0.092 V of bulk drop).
problems.trap: Subtracting the bulk drop from the knee and then dividing by $R_L$ alone — that double-counts $r_B$ and gives 9.21 mA only by accident of the numbers. Use $I = (V_{DD} - V_{knee})/(R_L + r_B)$: the bulk resistance limits the current, so it must appear where the total series resistance appears.

problems.prompt: For the $10\ \mathrm{V}$, $1\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$ silicon-diode circuit, state the load-line intercepts and locate the Q point both by the constant-drop model and by the actual Shockley curve with $I_S = 1\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{A}$.
steps: Intercepts: at $I_D = 0$, $V_D = V_{DD} = 10\ \mathrm{V}$; at $V_D = 0$, $I_D = 10/1000 = 10\ \mathrm{mA}$. The line has slope $-1/R_L$ and every valid answer lies inside that box.

Test against the real curve at $V_D = 0.6\ \mathrm{V}$: the diode wants $1\times10^{-12}e^{0.6/0.026} = 10.5\ \mathrm{mA}$, but the load line permits only $(10-0.6)/1000 = 9.4\ \mathrm{mA}$ — so the true Q sits at a lower voltage.
Test at $V_D = 0.59\ \mathrm{V}$: diode current $1\times10^{-12}e^{22.69} = 7.16\ \mathrm{mA}$ against 9.41 mA permitted — now too low, so Q is between 0.59 and 0.60 V.
Interpolate: at 0.5971 V both the diode and the load line give 9.403 mA, so Q $= (0.5971\ \mathrm{V}, 9.40\ \mathrm{mA})$.
problems.ans: Intercepts: (10 V, 0 mA) and (0 V, 10 mA). Constant-drop Q = (0.7 V, 9.3 mA); true Q = (0.5971 V, 9.40 mA).
problems.trap: Reading the knee point as the answer. The constant-drop model moves the Q point *along* the load line, so with a 1 kohm resistor the current error is only 1% — but the voltage error is 0.1 V, a 17% error in the diode voltage itself. With a 100 ohm resistor the same 0.1 V would move 1 mA (about 10% of the current), and any question asking specifically for $V_{DQ}$ wants the real intersection.

steps: Intercepts first: `(10 V, 0 mA)` and `(0 V, 10 mA)` bracket every legal answer.
calc.note: The constant-drop Q (0.7 V, 9.3 mA) is 17 % high in voltage even though the current is right to 1 %.

problems.prompt: Two diodes in series with a $1\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$ resistor are connected across $12\ \mathrm{V}$. Find the current when (i) both are silicon and (ii) one is silicon and one is germanium.
problems.ans: (i) I = 10.6 mA with 10.6 V across R. (ii) I = 11.0 mA with 11.0 V across R.
problems.trap: Applying one 0.7 V drop to a two-diode string: that gives 11.3 mA, about 7% high. The mirror-image trap is applying 0.7 V to the germanium diode, which is really 0.3 V; and do not run the series sum through the exponential, since the two junctions are at different temperatures and injection levels and the simple constant-drop model is the consistent choice.

steps: `(12−1.0)÷1000` → **11.0** mA for one silicon plus one germanium ($0.7+0.3$).
calc.note: Series knees add; one 0.7 V drop for the whole string is about 7 % high.

problems.prompt: A red LED has a nominal $V_F = 2.0\ \mathrm{V}$ and must run at $I_F = 20\ \mathrm{mA}$ from a $5\ \mathrm{V}$ supply. Find the series resistor, its power dissipation and the nearest standard value.
steps: $R = 150\ \Omega$ (a standard E12 value, so no rounding is needed).
$P_R = I_F^{2}R = (0.020)^{2}(150) = 0.060\ \mathrm{W}$; a 1/8 W (0.125 W) part is adequate, 1/4 W gives more margin.
problems.ans: R = 150 ohm, P_R = 60 mW (use 1/8 W or larger); the LED dissipates 40 mW.
problems.trap: Computing $R = V_S/I_F = 250\ \Omega$ and ignoring $V_F$; the LED then gets only 12 mA and runs dim. The subtler trap is designing at exactly the rated 20 mA with a nominal $V_F$: if $V_F$ falls to 1.8 V the current becomes $(5-1.8)/150 = 21.3\ \mathrm{mA}$, and if the 5 V rail is really 5.25 V it becomes 21.7 mA — both above the usual 20 mA rating, so a 160 or 180 ohm resistor is the safer design choice.

steps: `20E-3²×150` → **0.060** W in the resistor and `2×20E-3` → **40** mW in the LED.
calc.note: $R = V_S/I_F = 250$ $\Omega$ ignores $V_F$ and under-drives the LED at 12 mA.

traps: **Using the constant-drop model for a small signal.** A 50 mV sensor swing never turns on a 0.7 V battery model, so the model predicts no output at all, while the real diode is a linear 26 ohm resistor at 1 mA. Any question whose signal is comparable to $nV_T$ needs the dynamic model, not the knee.

**Putting $r_B$ outside the current equation.** The piecewise-linear current is $I = (V_{DD} - V_{knee})/(R_L + r_B)$, not $(V_{DD} - V_{knee} - Ir_B)/R_L$ evaluated with the wrong I. The bulk resistance limits current; it is a series element, not a post-hoc correction.

**Forgetting the diode drop when it is a large share of the supply.** The ideal model is 7% wrong on a 10 V loop but 88% wrong on a 1.5 V loop. Judge the model by the ratio $V_{knee}/V_{DD}$, not by habit.

**Assuming diodes in parallel share current.** The lower-drop or hotter device takes nearly all of it, because the forward voltage falls about $2\ \mathrm{mV/^\circ C}$ and the current is exponential in voltage. Parallel diodes need series ballast resistors or matched, thermally coupled parts.

**Sloppy kohm/mA bookkeeping.** $V/R$ with V in volts and R in kohm gives mA directly, which is why the shortcut is so common — but it silently breaks the moment one resistance is written in ohms. Write the units on every line of a load-line problem.

**Treating the Q point as immune to temperature.** The whole diode curve slides left by about $2\ \mathrm{mV/^\circ C}$, so at fixed $V_{DD}$ and $R_L$ the operating current *rises* as the diode heats. That positive feedback is exactly how a badly designed diode string thermally runs away.
